    Topic 2: Variables, mutability, and shadowing

    By the end, you will be able to

    • Declare immutable and mutable bindings.
    • Distinguish mutation from shadowing.
    • Define a typed constant.

    Prerequisite: Topic 1: Fundamentals overview.

    Names and change

    A variable gives a value a name. Rust infers many types, but function interfaces and ambiguous values need explicit types. A binding is immutable by default.

    let mut attempts: u8 = 2;
attempts += 1;             // Mutation requires mut.
let attempts = attempts.to_string(); // Shadowing creates a new binding.
println!("{attempts}");

    Shadowing with another let can change the type; assigning to an existing mut binding cannot change its type. Use const LIMIT: usize = 10; for a named constant whose value is computed at compile time.

    Checkpoint 1

    Why is the final let attempts = attempts.to_string() allowed?




    A constant needs an explicit type and a compile-time value. For example, const LIMIT: usize = 10; does not create a mutable counter.

    Can assigning to a mutable integer binding change its type to text?




    Runnable example

    fn main() {
    const LIMIT: usize = 10;
    let mut attempts: usize = 2;
    attempts += 1;
    assert_eq!(attempts, 3);
    assert!(attempts < LIMIT);
    let attempts = attempts.to_string();
    assert_eq!(attempts, "3");
    println!("attempts: {attempts}, limit: {LIMIT}");
}

    Run from the repository root:

    rustc examples/01-fundamentals/02-variables-mutability-shadowing/main.rs -o /tmp/rust-fundamentals-2
/tmp/rust-fundamentals-2

    Expected output:

    attempts: 3, limit: 10

    Exercise

    Start the counter at 4, increase it by 2, and update the assertions. Remove mut, read the error, then restore it. Explain why shadowing still needs a new let even when the original binding is mutable.

    Check your understanding

    Which choice creates a new binding?
